narrative:
The 2017 Chicago Cubs arrived as defending World Series champions, carrying the weight of expectation that comes with a title. April was an encouraging if uneven beginning — Willson Contreras launched a three-run shot on opening weekend, Kyle Schwarber announced himself with a three-run blast days later, and Anthony Rizzo delivered clutch hit after clutch hit. But the bullpen showed early cracks, most painfully when Pedro Strop surrendered a three-run homer to Andrew McCutchen that erased a late lead. Still, the Cubs finished April a respectable 13-11, with enough heroics to suggest the machine was humming.

May brought genuine turbulence. The Cubs stumbled to a 12-16 mark — their worst month of the season — and the bullpen's fragility became undeniable. Héctor Rondón's meltdown against New York, surrendering a three-run Brett Gardner homer that flipped the game, was the month's nadir. A plunking of Rizzo provided one brief, odd flash of fortune, but the Cubs were clearly not the dominant force of 2016. Yet June sparked a revival: Schwarber's grand slam in early June was a thunderclap, and Jon Jay's clutch double late in the month sent a message that this team still had fight. June closed 15-13, and the Cubs were steadying themselves.

July and August were when the Cubs truly rediscovered their championship identity. They went 16-8 in July, fueled by timely homers from Jon Jay and Addison Russell, before August brought a remarkable 17-12 run bookended by Willson Contreras's walk-off single and a clutch two-run hit from trade-deadline pickup Alex Avila. The bullpen — specifically Wade Davis — continued to show vulnerability, but the offense and the rotation kept the Cubs afloat. September was their finest month, a 19-9 surge that included Ian Happ's dramatic three-run walk-off blast on the final weekend, stamping their ticket and finishing 92-70.

October, however, belonged to heartbreak. The Cubs dispatched the Nationals in the NLDS but not without drama — Michael A. Taylor's grand slam off Davis in Game 3 and a follow-up homer in Game 4 were gut-punches that tested Chicago's resolve, before Addison Russell's double and a timely double play saved the series. Then came the Dodgers in the NLCS, and the dream unraveled quickly. Justin Turner's three-run homer off John Lackey in Game 1 set the tone for a series Chicago never truly controlled. The defending champions were eliminated, their title defense ending one round short of the Fall Classic.

chapters.title: Champions Return
chapters.description: The Cubs open the season with clutch homers and timely hits, posting a winning April despite early bullpen scares.

chapters.title: Stumbling Through May
chapters.description: A 12-16 May exposes bullpen vulnerabilities, with Rondón's meltdown against the Yankees epitomizing a difficult stretch.

chapters.title: Schwarber's Grand Slam and the June Turnaround
chapters.description: Schwarber's grand slam and Jon Jay's clutch double help the Cubs right the ship and close June at 15-13.

chapters.title: Winning Ugly All Summer
chapters.description: July and August see the Cubs grind out wins behind timely offense and clutch contributions from Russell, Contreras, and Avila despite continued bullpen wobbles.

chapters.title: September Surge
chapters.description: A dominant 19-9 September, capped by Happ's walk-off three-run blast, confirms the Cubs as a serious postseason contender.

chapters.title: October's Bitter End
chapters.description: The Cubs survive a dramatic NLDS against Washington before falling to the Dodgers in the NLCS, their title defense ending one round too soon.
